The approach emphasizes traceability, consistency, and compliance with safety-critical automotive development requirements. Validation is performed on a centralized vehicle computing platform supporting adaptive cruise control and emergency braking, tested in Hardware-in-the-Loop (HiL) and Software-in-the-Loop (SiL) environments. We discuss current capabilities, practical limitations, and future directions toward increasingly automated, reliable, and quality-assured automotive software development with minimal human intervention.

Software Engineering.title: VERDICT: Multi-Agent Parallel Modular Verification
Software Engineering.summary:
Deductive verification scales to large software systems through modular reasoning, where formal contracts summarize the behavior of individual functions and enable their independent verification. Its central bottleneck is specification synthesis: constructing the contracts required for modular verification. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated specification synthesis at unprecedented scale. However, existing approaches remain fundamentally bottom-up, requiring callees to be verified before their callers. This dependency limits parallelism and provides no principled mechanism for resolving interprocedural inconsistencies that propagate across call chains.
  We present VERDICT, a multi-agent framework for parallelizing modular deductive verification of large-scale programs. VERDICT is built on two key principles. First, assumption-based parallel specification synthesis assigns an agent to each function and allows it to proceed immediately using assumed contracts for its callees, enabling verification to proceed in parallel across the program. Second, bidirectional interprocedural conflict reconciliation resolves the inconsistencies introduced by these assumptions: when a synthesized contract contradicts an assumption, agents propagate the necessary revisions both up and down the call graph until the contracts converge. Experimental results on real-world C programs show that VERDICT synthesizes higher-quality specifications than existing approaches while substantially reducing verification time. In particular, VERDICT is the first approach that scales to the complete 20,000-line X.509 parser, ruling out nearly all the potential runtime errors within hours, whereas prior tools like PREGUSS fall far short even after days of execution.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at ICSE 2027

Software Engineering.title: ORSMT: Unleashing the Potential of Satisfiability Modulo Theories for Semantic Verification and Repair in LLM-Based Optimization
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models increasingly automate optimization modeling from natural language problems, producing written mathematics, solver code and a returned report. Verifying one optimization problem across these artifacts requires semantic comparison: unequal models can attain the same objective, equivalent models can use different auxiliary variables, and mutually consistent artifacts can omit the same source requirement. ORSMT provides a typed semantic interface and exact SMT relation queries. It aligns observable decisions, projects auxiliary variables, proves or refutes feasible region and objective relations, localizes refutations to implicated rows or domains and links source texts when available. It then reconstructs one artifact from another, and each adopted candidate passes the required relation checks. Across 3,034 problems and six generator sizes, ORSMT improves the model-code match rate in all 72 benchmark and generator combinations before selection. Protected selection raises the aggregate rate from 43.2% to 88.2% and the share that are both correct and matched from 25.2% to 40.2%. On the 1,905 refuted outputs, certified voting under the shared fallback makes 50.9% of outputs correct and matched, compared with 44.8% for ReLoop and 49.4% for Opt-Verifier. A separate one-round source revision followed by exact reconstruction restores a model-code match for 84.4% of the refuted pairs.

Software Engineering.title: VeeReview: Measuring Build-Verify Pairs in Agent-Authored Pull Requests from a V-Model Perspective
Software Engineering.summary: Context: Reviewing a pull request requires verification evidence that addresses the proposed change. Coding agent benchmarks and studies of pull request outcomes do not directly assess this relationship. Objective: We test whether the V-Model's build and verify pairs can measure verification evidence in pull requests and support comparisons between agent-authored and human-authored changes. Method: VeeReview classifies four build and verify pairs using repository signals and a language-model judge. Three pairs use model judgements constrained by deterministic signals, and a rule over the diff and repository tree decides Module Design-Unit Test. We evaluated VeeReview against a 25-pull request reference set labelled by two raters and applied it to 1,454 matched pairs of agent and human pull requests from 741 repositories. Results: VeeReview assigned lower build-only rates to agent-authored pull requests on all four pairs, contrary to the preregistered hypothesis (mixed-effects odds ratios 0.52 to 0.86). Architecture-Integration was not significant. Standardization for linked issues, shipped tests and size reduced matched-rate differences by 34% to 60%, and the rule-decided pair's standardized interval included zero. The instrument did not meet its preregistered calibration criterion: agreement with adjudicated labels was 4% to 60% against a required 80%, and inter-rater agreement was weak (kappa = 0.154). Conclusions: The rule-decided pair shows that a process measure judged by a language model partly reflects how a pull request is presented rather than the verification work behind it. We report the cohort differences as observations made with this instrument, and we argue that such measures need a mechanically decided component and a validated human reference before they can support comparisons of verification practice.
Software Engineering.comment: 47 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables. Under review at Empirical Software Engineering. Replication package: https://zenodo.org/records/22884519

Software Engineering.title: Symmetry-Oriented Testing Framework for Variational Quantum Algorithms
Software Engineering.summary:
Testing quantum software is challenging because quantum states cannot be directly inspected. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) are a particularly important target as they are among the most promising approaches for near-term noisy quantum hardware. Many testing methods rely on classically computed results, which conflicts with the regime where quantum advantage is expected. Although prior studies mitigate this oracle problem, the core difficulty remains that existing approaches do not verify whether the execution deviates from the intended problem or whether the obtained solution is physically plausible.
  We propose a symmetry-oriented testing framework for VQAs that addresses this gap by using operators commuting with the target Hamiltonian as test specifications. The framework provides two complementary diagnostics: a commutator-based health check that monitors whether each execution step during optimization remains consistent with the symmetry of the target Hamiltonian, and a variance-based acceptance check that assesses the converged solution by examining whether the state is an eigenstate of the symmetry operators. Both diagnostics derive from the problem structure and do not require the exact solution.
  We evaluate the framework on representative user- and system-side faults, across multiple target systems, and under injected noise. Results show that the two diagnostics detect faulty behavior, provide informative signals of solution quality, and remain useful under noisy execution.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 3 tables. Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Computing and Engineering (QCE26), Toronto, Canada, September 2026. Code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21405151

Software Engineering.title: VeriEvolve: Evaluator-First Evolution for Tool-Using Agents
Software Engineering.summary:
A central obstacle to self-improving agents is the absence of a reliable fitness signal for realistic stateful tasks. We introduce \textsc{VeriEvolve}, an evaluator-first evolution framework that constructs this missing evaluation layer before optimizing the agent. From task instruction, VeriEvolve synthesizes instruction-grounded challenge states and an executable evaluator that checks them. During each round of workflow evolution, the evaluator is frozen and serves as the fitness signal. Between rounds, VeriEvolve revises the evaluator by converting the end states of strong and weak runs into a pair of counterfactual test cases.
  Across all 30 MCPMark Filesystem tasks, VeriEvolve constructs 30 evaluators with 141 challenge states, achieving 141/141 agreement on the generated suites and 113/122 agreement on held-out states produced by executor agents. Evaluator-guided evolution increases externally verified success from 6/30 to 18/30 for GLM-5.2 and from 27/30 to 30/30 for Claude; refinement removes all three false positives that the weak executor exposes. Cross-environment studies on PostgreSQL, Playwright, Notion, and GitHub further expose complementary limits from observability, state representation, and search/execution capacity. These results show that executable evaluators can be synthesized and used to guide search when task success is observable and an external verifier is available for calibration.
Software Engineering.comment: 24 pages, 3 figures. Accepted to the REALM Workshop at EMNLP 2026 (non-archival)

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Beyond MSE: Rician Likelihood Denoising for Self-Supervised Cardiac $T2$ and $T1ρ$ MRI
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging involves an inherent trade-off among spatial resolution, acquisition time, and noise. This trade-off contributes to long scan times and high cost. Deep learning has improved image denoising, but cardiac MRI remains difficult because high-resolution, rapid acquisitions generally lack corresponding low-noise ground truth. Self-supervised denoising offers a potential solution by learning from noisy image pairs or even single noisy acquisitions. However, we show that Noise2Void-style blind-spot denoising, which uses a mean squared error (MSE) loss and assumes zero-mean, independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) noise, is poorly suited to MR magnitude images. When applied to short-axis $T2$-weighted and $T1ρ$-weighted cardiac MRI with synthetic Rician noise, it produces biased denoised images and biased parametric maps of $T2$ and $T1ρ$. To address this limitation, we formulate self-supervised denoising as maximum likelihood estimation under a known Rician noise model. This yields unbiased denoisers that are competitive with supervised baselines.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Made minor spelling and punctuation corrections

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: What Do Verifiable Rewards Teach Video-Language Models About Time? A Controlled Multi-Model Study
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) has produced large reasoning gains in language models, and verifiable video benchmarks make it applicable to causal-temporal video question answering. We study what RLVR teaches video-language models about time. We fine-tune four open models (Qwen3-VL-8B/4B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, Gemma-3-12B) with group relative policy optimization under three data recipes: verified (synthetic CLEVRER questions with exact answer and event-order rewards), unverified (self-supervised pretext tasks over 43,751 real web videos), and a 1:1 mixture, plus a verified+real arm that adds 4,000 verifiable questions on real video. Each cell is evaluated in-domain and on out-of-domain real video (a NExT-QA temporal stress set and an MVBench subset), with frames in order, shuffled, and absent. (1) Verified training yields large in-domain gains that shrink as base competence grows (+14 to +19 points on weaker models; +6 on the strongest). (2) Much of the gain is non-visual: accuracy with no frames rises nearly as much as with frames. (3) Verified-only training can severely degrade out-of-domain accuracy with no sign during training: Qwen3-VL-8B loses 26.7 and 25.2 points on the two real-video sets, while the mixture never significantly degrades a model trained on it. Adding real verified questions removes that loss (-2.3 points, within noise of base) and keeps a +9.3 in-domain gain, so the cause is narrow synthetic-only data, not verification. (4) No recipe induces temporal-order grounding: across 41 evaluations the ordered-versus-shuffled gap is indistinguishable from zero in 39 and marginal in two, despite an event-order reward. Verifiable rewards improve benchmark accuracy without temporal understanding. Report no-frame controls, and mix in real video to guard against out-of-domain degradation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Unified Trajectory and 3D Pose Forecasting for Multi-Agent Sports Analysis
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Forecasting future human motion requires jointly reasoning about an agent's global trajectory and 3D body pose, which are tightly coupled, particularly in team sports where multiple interacting players introduce complex social dynamics. We exploit a socio-temporal encoder that fuses trajectory and pose at the input level and models them jointly through shared factorized attention. The model is further enhanced by a per-joint loss reweighting scheme that emphasizes dynamic joints and prevents degenerate solutions, and a frequency-domain trajectory smoothing term that improves trajectory prediction while indirectly benefiting pose forecasting. To ensure fair comparison with prior joint forecasting methods, we identify and correct evaluation biases arising from overlapping sequence construction, adopting instead a non-overlapping protocol and a deterministic, oracle-free strategy for multi-future prediction. Our approach improves over prior joint forecasting methods on both WorldPose and 3DPW, with the largest gains on pose accuracy, demonstrating that the proposed joint formulation generalizes beyond the densely interactive scenarios that motivate it.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Principles of Robot Autonomy
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Autonomous robots are moving rapidly from research labs into everyday life - on roads, in the air, in warehouses, and in space. Robot autonomy is no longer solely an academic pursuit, but a collection of mature, field-tested methods and tools that practitioners rely on in real-world deployments. This book offers a clear, unified introduction to the methods that make this possible. Built on decades of teaching at Stanford, the text develops the core elements of modern autonomy stacks within a single conceptual framework, bridging classical robotics and modern physical AI. Every major topic is paired with hands-on Jupyter notebooks and implementation-driven exercises, so readers build practical intuition alongside theoretical understanding. The result is a principled, accessible, and deployment-aware foundation for anyone seeking to design, analyze, or contribute to the next generation of autonomous systems. This is a comprehensive resource for students, engineers, and researchers entering one of today's fastest-growing fields.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 531 pages. Pre-publication version of a book forthcoming from Cambridge University Press, posted with the permission of the publisher

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AVAtt: A Free-Viewing Eye-Tracking Dataset and Benchmark for Visual Attention on Paintings
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary:
Saliency and scanpath models are developed almost exclusively on natural photographs, yet paintings are composed by artists to guide the viewer's eye and differ from photographs in texture, colour and abstraction. We introduce \avatt, a free-viewing eye-tracking dataset on 
Images{} paintings spanning sixteen art movements and five centuries, with 
Scanpaths{} scanpaths and 
Fixations{} fixations from 
Participants{} participants (\spPerImageMin--\spPerImageMax{} observers per painting). For every painting we release individual scanpaths with fixation timing and eye--screen distance, fixation maps, saliency maps smoothed at one degree of visual angle, temporal saliency videos and rich art metadata. We benchmark classic and deep saliency models against human agreement, revealing substantial headroom for art-aware models, and rank 44 scanpath-similarity measures, including a new language-free family of image-encoder metrics built on ten CNN, ViT and self-supervised encoders. With controls that remove viewing biases, we show that faces are fixated  aceEnrich$	imes$ more than expected and within half a second, that local structure draws the eye, that composition rules fitted from image content predict where people look, and that art style shapes how much viewers agree. Dataset, code and a Python package are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Amine-CV/AVAtt.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: UniMem: Unifying Visual and Textual Memory in VLAs for Non-Markovian Tasks
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: While Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have leveraged internet-scale pretraining and task-specific finetuning to achieve strong performance on long-horizon tasks, they often struggle with non-Markovian tasks that require memory. Existing approaches to memory typically involve additional Vision-Language-Models (VLMs) for long-term memory management, introducing a memory bottleneck and a fractured training pipeline. Conditioning on multiple historical frames can provide the VLA with access to more descriptive features of past scenes, but can degrade performance if frames are chosen at arbitrary, fixed intervals. To address these limitations, we present UniMem, a framework that unifies high-level visual and textual memory and low-level control under one backbone. UniMem employs an event classifier to initiate textual and visual memory updates, a keyframe encoder for dense visual memory, and a keyframe caching technique to minimize overhead during policy rollouts. We evaluate UniMem across five simulation and four hardware tasks targeting sequential and spatial memory, demonstrating that our unified, single-model system outperforms fixed-interval image sampling baselines (93.4% vs. 68.2%) in simulation and hierarchical VLM-VLA baselines (80.0% vs. 43.5%) in hardware, while offering faster inference and a simple training pipeline for easy adoption. Project website: https://losterberg3.github.io/unimem-vla/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: SplatLab: Autonomous Scientific Discovery for 3DGS Research
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Reproducing a published 3DGS paper takes weeks of expert engineering before any extension can be proposed. Prior autonomous-research systems read papers, draft hypotheses, and write code, but are limited by short fixed templates, low executability, and weak traceability, and none has been demonstrated end-to-end in a live computer-vision subfield with intense activity. SplatLab is an autonomous research system for 3D Gaussian Splatting that addresses these limitations. Given a research prompt, a target-paper URL, or no input at all, it reproduces a published baseline, proposes an extension, trains and ablates across Mip-NeRF 360 and LLFF, writes the manuscript, and binds every reported number to a logged training run. Five design choices distinguish it: (i) candidates mutate plugins from a verified-reproduction backbone matched to published baselines; (ii) a cascade-weighted Elo tournament across eight islands scores candidates on measured GPU PSNR with verbal-gradient feedback; (iii) a standing falsifier subtracts Elo on failure, integrating stress-test survival into selection; (iv) every reported number is bound to a logged training run, and the run cannot terminate while any claim is unbacked; (v) a seven-category 3DGS taxonomy wraps EVOLVE-BLOCK markers in domain-aligned scaffolds transferable across 3DGS repositories. On PSNR-targeted runs, SplatLab's manuscripts beat their reproduced targets by +0.18 to +3.78 dB, including +3.78 dB on astrophotographic nebula rendering, for which no prior 3DGS method exists. The research cycle compresses from months of graduate-student time to days of mostly autonomous compute. Code, all manuscripts, experiment ledgers, and the cross-run paper store are available on the project page.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 14 pages, 4 figures. Project page: https://seemandhar.github.io/splatlab

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Where to Look Is Not How to Fix: Pre-Denoising Diagnostics and Modality-Dependent Control in Diffusion Composition
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Understanding compositional failures in text-to-image diffusion requires identifying both where stress is detectable and how intervention changes the output. We study these questions through a controlled anchor--stress protocol that jointly evaluates text-encoder diagnostics and denoiser interventions. We introduce a text-only Compositional Stress Index (CSI), which separates common from rare compositions across SD1.5, SDXL, and the SD3 text path and provides an upstream diagnostic coordinate. A matched six-prompt localization study links intervention location to distinct outcomes: residual-minimizing embedding adapters improve representation fit, while downstream cross-attention intervention increases color hit rate (CHR) by 0.0272. Across SD1.5 and SDXL denoiser blocks, the largest positive signed diagnostic-accessibility mean occurs at the deep encoder, whereas selective boost has its largest positive mean CHR response at decoder blocks. Selective subtraction and broad ablation reveal further modality- and architecture-dependent responses, including a substantial CHR decrease when SDXL decoder cross-attention is broadly ablated. We find a diagnosis-control dissociation under our controlled attribute-object composition setting: compositional defects are diagnosable before denoising, but the representation coordinate that exposes risk is not necessarily the coordinate or modality that improves generation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Learning from Automatic 3D Gaussian Splatting Edits for Online Bayesian Scene Change Detection
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to a reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning offline from automatic edits to a reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene-specific evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed-form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian field. Object-guided refinement produces the final change masks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with $67.64\%$ and $75.82\%$ mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at $17.2$\,FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods. Project page: https://changruizhu96.github.io/work/lego-scd/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MAVOS-DD: Multilingual Audio-Video Open-Set Deepfake Detection Benchmark
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We present the first large-scale open-set benchmark for multilingual audio-video deepfake detection. Our dataset comprises nearly 350 hours of real and fake videos across eight languages, with 59% of data being generated. For each language, the fake videos are generated with several distinct audio and video deepfake generation models, selected based on their quality, via visual inspection. We organize the training, validation and test splits such that only a subset of the chosen generative models and languages are available during training, thus creating several challenging open-set evaluation setups. We perform experiments with various pre-trained and fine-tuned deepfake detectors proposed in recent literature. Our results show that state-of-the-art detectors are not currently able to maintain their performance levels when tested in our open-set scenarios. We publicly release our data and code for non-commercial use at https://github.com/CroitoruAlin/MAVOS-DD.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Measuring Pretraining Contamination in Public Medical Vision-Language Benchmarks
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are evaluated on public benchmarks whose images and question-answer pairs have been freely available for years, yet reported accuracy assumes that these examples were not in the training data. We test this assumption for open VLMs on SLAKE-En, PathVQA, and VQA-RAD, and on a public mirror of OmniMedVQA, using four detectors: image near-neighbour search against PMC-OA-beta, canonical-order exchangeability, cohort-relative Min-K%++ tail enrichment, and cross-model top-K overlap. On the image side, 19.8% of SLAKE-En images have an unusually close neighbour in PMC-OA-beta under SigLIP-B-16 (4.2% under SigLIP-SO400M), while out-of-domain control images produce no flags. Manual inspection shows that these are images of the same modality and view from different patients, not exact copies, so we read the signal as overlap in image sources rather than memorization of individual images. On the text side, Qwen2.5-VL shows an exchangeability signal on SLAKE-En that survives an ordering ablation and two non-medical baseline models, and on the OmniMedVQA mirror exchangeability fires for five medical and general VLMs while BLIP-2 does not. The other two detectors fail a simple control: BLIP-2, which has no plausible exposure to medical VQA data, reproduces their apparent positive signals. Cohort-relative Min-K%++ and top-K overlap are therefore unreliable as standalone contamination signals for small groups of medical VLMs and should be checked against an outside baseline model.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: RiskCueBench: Benchmarking Anticipatory Reasoning from Early Risk Cues in Video-Language Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: With the rapid growth of video centered social media, the ability to anticipate risky events from visual data is a promising direction for ensuring public safety and preventing real world accidents. Prior work has extensively studied supervised video risk assessment across domains such as driving, protests, and natural disasters. However, many existing datasets provide models with access to the full video sequence, including the accident itself, which substantially reduces the difficulty of the task. To better reflect real world conditions, we introduce a new video understanding benchmark RiskCueBench in which videos are carefully annotated to identify a risk signal clip, defined as the earliest moment that indicates a potential safety concern. Experimental results reveal a significant gap in current systems ability to interpret evolving situations and anticipate future risky events from early visual signals, highlighting important challenges for deploying video risk prediction models in practice.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VisCurate: Evaluating Behavioral Equivalence of Visual Skills
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Modern vision-based agents have shifted toward skill-based problem-solving, where a skill is an executable image-to-image operation, e.g., cropping, thresholding, or edge detection. As these skill libraries grow, they accumulate duplicated, mislabeled, and defective skills. The signals normally used to curate them (a skill's name, description, or source code) say little about how the skill visually changes the image. We present VisCurate, a framework and benchmark that curates visual skill libraries from observed execution rather than from text. VisCurate runs each candidate skill pair on a shared probe battery and assigns one of six behavioral relations, each tied to a library edit that is safe to make. The benchmark injects seven defect types into a clean library at controlled rates, producing 300 reproducible instances with ground-truth relations and repairs. While text baselines accept up to five of six false merges on hard negatives, our verifier accepts none and recovers 51.2% of the pairs that are truly mergeable. On two real, uncurated libraries, VisCurate finds that 92% of the skills a package shares with its downstream copy are redundant, while execution confirms only 10 of 17 published equivalence claims. The curation problem also remains open, as the strongest of the nine automated curators recovers only about half of the repairs. We emphasize that visual skill libraries should be curated by behavior, not by description.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Accepted at the IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV 2027), Main Conference

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Latent Space Jam: Layout Guided Video Synthesis
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Adding control to video generation often requires training, which demands additional computational resources, data, or architectural changes. We propose a training-free approach that utilizes pretrained video diffusion models to control object layout and motion using coarse layouts. Our method operates in two passes: first, it steers spatiotemporal placement through prompt-guided cross-attention to produce a coarse visual guide; second, this guide conditions the same model to generate a high-quality, layoutconsistent video. The approach enables coordinated motion with strong temporal consistency, supporting diverse trajectories and object interactions without additional training. Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms prior work in overlap and trajectory accuracy, as well as visual quality across static, dynamic, and multi-object scene settings.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Closing the Navigation Compliance Gap in End-to-end Autonomous Driving
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Trajectory-scoring planners achieve high navigation compliance when following the expert's original command, yet they struggle at intersections when presented with alternative commands; over 30 percent of such commands are ignored. We attribute this navigation compliance gap to two root causes: (1) existing metrics like Ego Progress do not explicitly measure navigation adherence, diluting the gap between on-route and off-route trajectories; and (2) current datasets pair each scenario with a single command, preventing models from learning command-dependent behavior. We address the metric gap by introducing the binary Navigation Compliance metric (NAVI) and the derived Controllability Measure (CM), and the data gap with the NavControl dataset, 14,918 intersection scenarios augmented with all feasible alternative commands and routing annotations, yielding over 34,000 direction samples. Building on these, we propose NaviHydra, a trajectory-scoring planner incorporating NAVI distillation and Bird's Eye View (BEV)-based trajectory gathering for context-position-aware trajectory feature extraction. NaviHydra achieves 92.7 PDM score on NAVSIM navtest split and 77.5 CM on NavControl test split. Training with NavControl improves controllability across diverse architectures, confirming it as a broadly effective augmentation for navigation compliance. Our project page is https://hanfeng-wu.github.io/closing/.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MeSS: City Mesh-Guided Outdoor Scene Generation with Cross-View Consistent Diffusion
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Mesh models have become increasingly accessible for numerous cities; however, the lack of realistic textures restricts their application in virtual urban navigation and autonomous driving. To address this, this paper proposes MeSS (Meshbased Scene Synthesis) for generating high-quality, styleconsistent outdoor scenes with city mesh models serving as the geometric prior. While image and video diffusion models can leverage spatial layouts (such as depth maps or HD maps) as control conditions to generate street-level perspective views, they are not directly applicable to 3D scene generation. Video diffusion models excel at synthesizing consistent view sequences that depict scenes but often struggle to adhere to predefined camera paths or align accurately with rendered control videos. In contrast, image diffusion models, though unable to guarantee cross-view visual consistency, can produce more geometry-aligned results when combined with ControlNet. Building on this insight, our approach enhances image diffusion models by improving cross-view consistency. The pipeline comprises three key stages: first, we generate geometrically consistent sparse views using Cascaded Outpainting ControlNets; second, we propagate denser intermediate views via a component dubbed AGInpaint; and third, we globally eliminate visual inconsistencies (e.g., varying exposure) using the GCAlign module. Concurrently with generation, a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene is reconstructed by initializing Gaussian balls on the mesh surface. Our method outperforms existing approaches in both geometric alignment and generation quality. Once synthesized, the scene can be rendered in diverse styles through relighting and style transfer techniques. project page: https://albertchen98.github.io/mess/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: FiLM-CAM: Keyed Feature Modulation for Conditional-Access Watermarking
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We propose FiLM-CAM; a conditional-access image watermarking approach that enforces authorized encoding, decoding, and removal through keyed feature modulation. A secret key conditions a Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM) mechanism that transforms the internal representation of the watermark signal before embedding, thereby coupling the payload to the key at the feature, rather than pixel level. The same key must be presented to condition the decoder to correctly recover the payload embedded in an image. To enforce conditional access, we train the system to maximize the performance gap between authorized and unauthorized use, ensuring reliable extraction under the correct key while inducing failure under incorrect keys. In addition, we design our encoder to estimate the watermark residual invariant to the presence of pre-existing watermarks. This design enables conditional watermark removal via simple re-encoding and subtraction of the residual using iterative refinement, contingent on knowledge of the secret key. We evaluate FiLM-CAM across multiple watermarking encoder-decoder backbones, demonstrating that keyed feature modulation serves as an effective, architecture-agnostic conditional access module (CAM) for image watermarking.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Foundation4D: Towards a unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: MoRE: Motion-Regularized Encoding for Articulated 3D Generation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Generating an articulated object from a single image requires recovering both its appearance and the mechanism governing its parts. A compact encoding of joint attributes does not by itself ensure that reconstruction preserves the resulting motion. We present MoRE, Motion-Regularized Encoding for articulated 3D generation. MoRE represents coordinate-aligned joint lines with axis classification and two axis-orthogonal Plücker moment coefficients, removing the arbitrary choice of an origin along the axis. During representation learning, decoded joint hypotheses are used to move corresponding three-dimensional anchors, and their motions are compared with those of annotated joints. A differentiable expectation over joint types and axis directions couples attribute reconstruction to the motion it induces. An image-conditioned flow learns the resulting functional latents, while a multi-state-adapted Gaussian model supplies appearance. At inference, recovered part assignments and joints articulate a single set of rest-pose Gaussians without regenerating the object for each state. Experiments on PartNet-Mobility and ACD show stronger part-box agreement, articulated-state geometry and visual similarity than the compared baselines, while joint prediction reduces axis, origin and range errors relative to ArtiLatent. Controlled ablations support the joint-line encoding and show that motion supervision reduces anchor-motion error. Code and pretrained checkpoints will be released in the future.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: R4DGS: Referring Segmentation in 4D Gaussian Splatting
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Dynamic representations based on 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) have shown strong capabilities in reconstruction and rendering, yet current methods remain limited in supporting complex natural-language referring in dynamic scenes. Existing 4D Gaussian methods are primarily designed for rendering-oriented dynamic modeling, while current semantic extensions often rely on scene-specific semantic optimization or are evaluated on relatively simple query settings. In this paper, we study Referring 4D Gaussian Splatting (R4DGS), a task for grounding temporally varying, multi-target or reasoning-intensive, and zero-target or distractor expressions in dynamic 4D scenes. To support this task, we introduce R4D-Bench-QA, a benchmark with structured query annotations. We further present ReferGaussian, a unified framework built upon 4DGS that converts low-level dynamic Gaussians into persistent, language-addressable entities for training-free referring inference. ReferGaussian organizes mask-supported Gaussian entities in an EntityBank, uses Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to decompose complex queries into trackable object phrases and structured referring constraints, and performs constraint-aware grounding without scene-specific semantic optimization. Experiments on R4D-Bench-QA and the 4D LangSplat protocol demonstrate improved temporal target selection and competitive spatiotemporal grounding without scene-specific semantic training. Project resources are available at https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 10 pages. Accepted at ACM Multimedia 2026. Project page: https://chenbangpu.github.io/R4DGS/

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EchoXFlow: A Beamspace Echocardiography Dataset for Cardiac Motion, Flow, and Function
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce EchoXFlow, a clinical echocardiography dataset with ultrasound in its native acquisition geometry. Existing public datasets offer limited opportunities to study how cardiac anatomy, myocardial motion, and blood flow relate: Doppler velocities are typically absent or fused as RGB overlays on grayscale anatomical images, and acquisitions are released only after scan conversion and lossy vendor display processing. EchoXFlow comprises 35,377 recordings from 666 routine-care examinations of 622 patients. It preserves the timing, geometry, and modality relationships needed for physically grounded echo learning. Each recording is retained as separable modality-specific streams: temporally resolved 1D, 2D, and 3D data alongside multiple Doppler modalities, paired with a synchronized ECG. Clinical annotations range from guideline-defined measurements to dense 2D myocardial contours and 3D left-ventricular endocardial meshes. With its associated open-source tooling, EchoXFlow enables cross-modal, acquisition-aware learning tasks that cannot be formulated from conventional scan-converted videos alone, and serves as a testbed for 4D vision and physically grounded multi-modal learning more broadly. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Ahus-AIM/EchoXFlow and the tooling at https://github.com/Ahus-AIM/EchoXFlow

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: EgoHand: Monocular 3D Hand Reconstruction from Egocentric Video
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: We introduce EgoHand, a monocular 3D hand reconstruction model that achieves state-of-the-art performance on egocentric video. Central to our approach is the curation of a high-quality training corpus of 14 million images, combining synthetic data, in-the-wild video, and multi-camera motion capture to balance scene diversity and supervision quality. The model adopts SOMA-Hand as its parametric representation and processes 2D hand crops with a transformer encoder, incorporating camera cues and an auxiliary 2D branch to improve geometric consistency and image alignment. Zero-shot evaluations on HOT3D, ARCTIC, and H2O demonstrate strong out-of-domain generalization, with lower joint-position, root-translation, and acceleration errors than competing baselines at an inference latency of approximately 9.69 ms. A blinded user preference study further shows that participants favor EgoHand's reconstructed hand poses over those from Apple EgoDex and Ropedia Xperience-10M. We release the EgoHand model and source code under the OpenMDW license, allowing free commercial use of the model.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: Authors are listed alphabetically. Project leads are Chao-Yeh Chen, Tiffany Chen, and Umar Iqbal

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Rethinking Video Autoencoders for Interactive World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Video world models predict future frames from past frames and actions. They serve as simulators in which agents train, plan or are evaluated, and that humans can control interactively. They generate in the latent space of a video autoencoder, whose compression sets their cost per frame and how long each action waits to take effect. Yet world models often reuse the autoencoders of text-to-video generators, built for offline generation with no agent waiting and, without their training data and code, not retrainable at another compression. We therefore ask how, where and how much a world model should compress. We build CADRE, an open family of causal diffusion representation autoencoders spanning multiple spatio-temporal compressions. Its members differ only in a small bottleneck on frozen features and share a diffusion decoder self-distilled to one or a few steps. We train the same world model on each autoencoder in two domains, manipulation and navigation, with two environments each. CADRE forms most of the latency-quality frontier, especially with a moving camera. Our study also leads to four findings. At strong compression, a diffusion decoder is sharper than perceptual regression. In robot manipulation, temporal compression is more effective in the autoencoder than in the world model. Manipulation and navigation call for opposite compressions: temporal compression costs little when the camera is still, and spatial compression when it moves. Surprisingly, with a still camera, coarser spatial tokens hurt motion far more than image quality. Code, models and a live demo are at https://kyutai.org/blog/2026-10-21-cadre

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: VoxProg: 3D Spatial Reasoning through Voxel Programming
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Language models' abilities to interpret tasks and generate programs offer a promising basis for 3D spatial reasoning. Yet following spatial instructions in 3D scenes requires programs to construct geometric references that language leaves implicit. In this work, we introduce VoxProg, which formulates 3D object placement through voxel programming: a language model translates task interpretations into executable programs over local voxel views of scene surfaces. Because these views index surface geometry on regular grids with explicit coordinates and neighborhood relations, an evidence program can isolate task-relevant regions and boundaries directly from scene meshes, and a downstream pose program can measure the resulting geometry to compute a target $SE(3)$ pose. Visual and numerical feedback from execution lets the model inspect intermediate selections and candidate placements to iteratively revise its code. To evaluate open-ended placement across functional use, geometric fit, and contextual arrangements, we introduce the 71-task VoxProg-Bench benchmark along with an evaluation suite pairing perceptual Intent Alignment and 3D Physical Validity. Across VoxProg-Bench and external benchmarks, VoxProg consistently outperforms relation-based, keypoint-based, and mesh-based baselines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: PhysiCalWorld: In-Context Physics Calibration for World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Existing world models typically perceive a scene through current visual frame or a narrow history window. However, these observations may not reveal the physics properties that determine transition dynamics, such as an object's mass distribution, joint damping, or surface friction. Without calibrating these physics factors for world models, predictions tend to regress toward an empirical prior and induce severe drift in novel test scenes. To this end, we propose PhysiCalWorld, which calibrates action-conditioned world models to the instance-specific dynamics via in-context prompting, without fine-tuning or analytical physics modeling. Our method encodes an exploratory interaction clip collected within the test scene into a compact physics descriptor token, which grounds subsequent predictions in the scene's actual physical behavior. PhysiCalWorld is trained end-to-end with the latent prediction loss alone, without physics labels. At inference time, the descriptor token is extracted once and can be reused across rollouts with negligible compute overhead. We evaluate PhysiCalWorld across four environments covering diverse physics variations and show that it substantially improves rollout prediction accuracy and visual planning success rate. The learned descriptors also form a physically structured latent space and generalize beyond the physics ranges seen during training.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: ALPS: Visual State Encoders for World Models
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: World models turn visual representations into predictions and actions. We argue that their visual foundation should combine physical-state information, native language alignment, and pixel reconstruction, so that a single representation can support prediction, instruction, and inspection. However, existing encoders typically specialize in only one or two of these capabilities; we therefore introduce ALPS, a pretrained visual state encoder that unifies all three in a single set of patch tokens. Using only still images and text, we pretrain a ViT-B/16 from scratch with language, reconstruction, and spatial correspondence objectives, and then refine it via cross-view self-distillation. In a unified evaluation across fifteen public encoders, ALPS achieves the lowest aggregate LIBERO state-probe error among ViT-B models (matching the 3.5x larger V-JEPA 2-L) while maintaining strong language alignment and accurate pixel reconstruction. Downstream, frozen ALPS tokens reach the highest mean policy success on LIBERO (85.5%) when paired with our native text tower, match or exceed leading encoders on world-model planning across PushT, Wall, and Granular, and allow predicted future tokens to be decoded directly into pixels for visual inspection. We hope this work helps establish visual pretraining as a shared foundation for understanding, prediction, and action in world models.
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.comment: 35 pages (15 main + 20 supplementary), 13 figures, 26 tables. Project page: https://ucsc-vlaa.github.io/ALPS/ Code: https://github.com/UCSC-VLAA/ALPS

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: Multimodal Embodied Agents: A Unified Capability-centric Perspective from Computer-Use to Robot-Use
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Multimodal agents (MMAs) sustain interaction through reasoning, memory, tools, and feedback, most visibly as computer-use agents, while robotic systems (RSs) couple sensing and actuation under physical dynamics. We define multimodal embodied agents (MMEAs) as goal-directed systems that couple multimodal task reasoning with physical action and revise decisions from the resulting feedback. This raises a central question: what changes when a multimodal agent moves from computer-use to robot-use? We introduce PAPAV, a unified capability-centric framework of five recurring functions: Perceive the current state, Anticipate action effects, Plan a feasible course, Act through an interface or body, and Verify the outcome. Defined by function rather than architecture, these capabilities let PAPAV identify what all three share and then compare MMEAs with MMAs and with RSs. Five physical constraints, from partial observability to unverifiable outcomes, leave fewer choices fixed in advance and less room to reverse errors. Across 64 benchmarks, explicit evaluation centers on Act; only 5 assess Anticipate and 3 assess Verify, leaving both largely hidden behind task success. These constraints also frame the open challenges we identify. PAPAV therefore provides a common basis for designing reliable physical agents and measuring progress across all five capabilities rather than task success alone.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: $\mathbf{R}^3$: Reconstruction, Raw, and Rain: Deraining Directly in the Bayer Domain
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Image reconstruction from corrupted images is crucial across many domains. Most reconstruction networks are trained on post-ISP sRGB images, even though the image-signal-processing pipeline irreversibly mixes colors, clips dynamic range, and blurs fine detail. This paper uses the rain degradation problem as a use case to show that these losses are avoidable, and demonstrates that learning directly on raw Bayer mosaics yields superior reconstructions. To substantiate the claim, we (i) evaluate post-ISP and Bayer reconstruction pipelines, (ii) curate Raw-Rain, the first public benchmark of real rainy scenes captured in both 12-bit Bayer and bit-depth-matched sRGB, and (iii) introduce Information Conservation Score (ICS), a color-invariant metric that aligns more closely with human opinion than PSNR or SSIM. On the test split, our raw-domain model improves sRGB results by up to +0.99 dB PSNR and +1.2% ICS, while running faster with half of the GFLOPs. The results advocate an ISP-last paradigm for low-level vision and open the door to end-to-end learnable camera pipelines.

Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.title: AtomicRL: Atomic Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown promise in robotic manipulation, but imitation learning (IL) alone often struggles to master complex long-horizon skills. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers an effective avenue for further improving VLA policies. However, existing VLA-RL methods typically suffer from delayed and biased credit assignment due to trajectory-level sparse rewards, while imbalanced subtask mastery creates bottlenecks that limit overall performance. To address these challenges, we propose AtomicRL, an RL post-training framework that leverages atomic task structures for reliable credit assignment and adaptive exploration. AtomicRL introduces Semantic-Aware Policy Optimization (SAPO), which uses semantic-aware gating to constrain TD residuals from failed atomic subtasks from propagating across task boundaries, mitigating credit contamination while preserving intra-subtask credit assignment and value bootstrapping. In addition, Bottleneck-Adaptive Target Exploration (BATE) dynamically coordinates task sampling and local exploration incentives based on the mastery of individual atomic subtasks, directing learning toward the remaining bottlenecks. Finally, we develop a Real2Sim2Real pipeline that bridges online RL in simulation with real-world deployment, facilitating practical transfer to physical robots. On LIBERO-LONG, AtomicRL achieves absolute performance gains of 3.6% and 4.0% over PPO across two VLA architectures. On CALVIN ABC-D, it improves full-task performance by up to 9.5% over PPO. Combined with the Real2Sim2Real pipeline, AtomicRL further improves real-world task performance by an average of 21.3%. These results demonstrate that AtomicRL effectively improves the learning efficiency and manipulation performance of VLA policies on long-horizon tasks.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: WaxalNet: Benchmarking and Adapting Speech Recognition for Spontaneous Speech in 19 African Languages
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Multilingual speech foundation models claim broad language coverage, but how well they handle spontaneous African speech, and how best to adapt them, remains unclear. We benchmark zero-shot and fine-tuned speech recognition on the WAXAL corpus of spontaneous speech in 19 African languages, covering Whisper, MMS, Omnilingual ASR, and SeamlessM4T-v2. Fine-tuning lowers macro word error rate (WER) from 52.3 for the best zero-shot model covering all 19 languages (Omnilingual-7B) to 36.2 for a 300M-parameter MMS model and 31.5 for Omnilingual with an LLM decoder, although zero-shot models are already competitive on a few languages. Using Omnilingual's shared encoder, we compare CTC and LLM decoders with encoder pretraining held fixed. Between MMS and Whisper, the better model depends on the language family, but with a shared encoder the LLM decoder has lower WER on 18 of 19 languages, so the family pattern more likely comes from pretraining than from the decoder. The LLM decoder is, however, about five times larger and much slower on CPU. Pooling languages into one model, by family or across all 19, costs only 0.6 to 1.0 WER on average relative to per-language models, a modest price for serving all languages with one model. Fine-tuned models remain usable on read speech, and for held-out languages neither training on the other languages nor in-context examples replace in-language fine-tuning. A native-speaker audit across all 19 languages characterizes failure modes such as repetition loops. We release the code and a suite of over 100 fine-tuned models.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: AVAtt: A Free-Viewing Eye-Tracking Dataset and Benchmark for Visual Attention on Paintings
Human-Computer Interaction.summary:
Saliency and scanpath models are developed almost exclusively on natural photographs, yet paintings are composed by artists to guide the viewer's eye and differ from photographs in texture, colour and abstraction. We introduce \avatt, a free-viewing eye-tracking dataset on 
Images{} paintings spanning sixteen art movements and five centuries, with 
Scanpaths{} scanpaths and 
Fixations{} fixations from 
Participants{} participants (\spPerImageMin--\spPerImageMax{} observers per painting). For every painting we release individual scanpaths with fixation timing and eye--screen distance, fixation maps, saliency maps smoothed at one degree of visual angle, temporal saliency videos and rich art metadata. We benchmark classic and deep saliency models against human agreement, revealing substantial headroom for art-aware models, and rank 44 scanpath-similarity measures, including a new language-free family of image-encoder metrics built on ten CNN, ViT and self-supervised encoders. With controls that remove viewing biases, we show that faces are fixated  aceEnrich$	imes$ more than expected and within half a second, that local structure draws the eye, that composition rules fitted from image content predict where people look, and that art style shapes how much viewers agree. Dataset, code and a Python package are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Amine-CV/AVAtt.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Neurophysiological Insights into Multimedia-based Education: A PRISMA-ScR Review of fNIRS in Game-Integrated Learning Systems
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Game-integrated learning systems (GILS) are a growing form of multimedia education. Neurophysiological evidence can complement behavioral and learning measures when examining how users interact with these environments. This scoping review follows PRISMA-ScR and synthesizes 20 empirical studies published between 2014 and 2025, identified through searches updated in April 2026, in which functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) measured task-related cortical hemodynamic responses during GILS use. The review maps learning contexts, multimedia platforms, outcome measures, and methodological approaches across the included studies. Individual studies reported differences in cortical responses across interaction conditions and associations with behavioral or learning outcomes. However, only 10 of the 20 studies assessed learning outcomes, and methodological heterogeneity limits cross-study comparisons. These findings do not establish that specific multimedia platforms cause particular neural or learning outcomes. Future research should prioritize standardized methods, ecologically valid learning settings, and evaluation of the feasibility and educational value of real-time neural adaptation.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: X-pressing Intimacy: Mental Health Disclosure After Twitter Acquisition
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Social media platforms provide spaces for individuals to disclose mental health experiences and seek support, yet how these disclosures evolve during major shifts in platform governance remains unclear. We examine mental health self-disclosure surrounding Elon Musk's October 2022 acquisition of Twitter, analyzing approximately 824K tweets across anxiety, depression, bipolar disorder (BD), borderline personality disorder (BPD), and suicidal ideation (SI) or related experiences, alongside 266K comparison tweets. Using Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC) and an LLM-based intimacy classifier, we characterize changes in psycholinguistic expression and disclosure intimacy. Following the acquisition, we observe declines in affective and social language, alongside increases in first-person singular pronouns and future-focused expressions. Intimacy patterns vary by condition: anxiety, depression, and BPD show increases in low-intimacy and decreases in moderate-intimacy disclosures, whereas suicide-related posts show more high-intimacy disclosures. However, compared with broader Twitter discourse, only the relative decline in moderate- versus low-intimacy disclosure for BPD remains statistically significant. Our findings underscore the importance of considering both language and intimacy when studying platform transitions, informing the design of online environments that support sensitive self-disclosure.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Data-Void Exploits in Web-Searching LLMs
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Extended version of the paper to appear in the Network and Distributed System Security (NDSS) Symposium 2027. 23 pages

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Exploring spatial configuration and group familiarity when co-watching 360-degree stories in social virtual reality
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: While traditional cinematic viewing is often characterized as a social experience, engaging with immersive stories is predominantly researched as an individual activity. This mismatch becomes increasingly problematic in social virtual reality (VR), where features designed for typical social activities (e.g., virtual locomotion, spatial and social context) can become meaningful levers for shaping the user experience. To address our limited understanding of these effects, we conducted three exploratory experiments (N$_1$=109, N$_2$=116, N$_3$=88) examining how spatial boundary type, size of allocated personal space, and group familiarity influence co-watching 360-degree stories in social VR. Results shows that small communal spatial boundaries heightened social presence towards others compared to individual boundaries, but also increased mental demand. Reducing the size of the personal spatial boundary increased social presence towards others but also increased disorientation and frustration. Finally, participants with higher group familiarity reported stronger attentional focus on the story, as well as higher spatial presence and social presence towards story characters, but also reported greater physical and perceptual demand. We discuss systematic tradeoffs between engagement and cognitive effort, and suggest practical guidelines for designing shared immersive narrative experiences.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Measurement-Guided Conversion of Laboratory Eye-Tracking Data for VR Authentication
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Eye-movement authentication in virtual reality (VR) needs longitudinal training data, yet most such datasets come from lab trackers. We convert lab recordings to a VR headset's signal quality while keeping their eye movement, using only unpaired VR recordings of other people. Measurements show that the headset's added noise dominates above 7.8 Hz and that its quality is consistent within a person. A parametric device model re-creates the headset's sampling, a person-consistent calibration error and spectrally shaped noise, and a frequency-locked diffusion renderer re-textures that high-frequency noise. Converted GazeBase recordings match GazeBaseVR in noise level and accuracy, keep their source's saccade dynamics, and are harder to tell from real VR data than two prior conversions. An authenticator trained only on converted data verifies unseen VR users at a 5.9% equal error rate with 45 s of gaze, close to real VR training (5.8%); with 5 s, a gap remains.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: RubRIX: Rubric-Driven Risk Mitigation in Caregiver-AI Interactions
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Caregivers seeking AI-mediated support express complex needs---information-seeking, emotional validation, and distress cues---that warrant careful evaluation of response safety and appropriateness. Existing AI evaluation frameworks, primarily focused on general risks (toxicity, hallucinations, policy violations, etc), may not adequately capture the nuanced risks of LLM-responses in caregiving-contexts. We introduce RubRIX (Rubric-based Risk Index), a theory-driven, clinician-validated framework for evaluating risks in LLM caregiving responses. Grounded in the Elements of an Ethic of Care, RubRIX operationalizes five empirically-derived risk dimensions: Inattention, Bias & Stigma, Information Inaccuracy, Uncritical Affirmation, and Epistemic Arrogance. We evaluate six state-of-the-art LLMs on over 20,000 caregiver queries from Reddit and ALZConnected. Rubric-guided refinement consistently reduced risk-components by 45-98% after one iteration across models. This work contributes a methodological approach for developing domain-sensitive, user-centered evaluation frameworks for high-burden contexts. Our findings highlight the importance of domain-sensitive, interactional risk evaluation for the responsible deployment of LLMs in caregiving support contexts. We release benchmark datasets to enable future research on contextual risk evaluation in AI-mediated support.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: TrustmeWatcher: An Application for Workplace Micro-Sensing and Explainable Well-Being Feedback
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Workplace sensing studies combine long-running behaviour traces with self-reports, yet the tools that collect those data often sit apart from the interface that returns results. We present TrustmeWatcher, the application built for the TRUST-ME project to connect this work. TrustmeWatcher reuses ActivityWatch's OS-level watchers for computer-activity collection and adds its own application layer. It turns the collected traces into an interactive screen-time dashboard, synchronizes responses from short questionnaires completed on the StreamDeck, and presents questionnaires alongside video highlights. Activity records and self-reports are aligned into labelled records for model development. The scope of this paper is limited to ActivityWatch data as model input. Artificial intelligence (AI) uses these activity records to predict six normalized state scores and an overall well-being score. The trained model runs locally, and the dashboard presents its predictions in semantic bands. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) helps users understand how recorded activity contributed to a prediction. Privacy Control lets users pause or resume the camera and eye tracker used by the study. We describe the workflow, its user-device and sensing-setup boundaries, and its use with records from 17 participants. The result is a deployed application and study workflow that integrates activity review, study data collection, privacy control, local prediction, and a participant-facing interface for XAI evaluation.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: 4 pages, 5 figures. Accepted at XAI for U 2026, the 3rd International Workshop on Explainable AI for Ubiquitous, Pervasive and Wearable Computing, co-located with UbiComp/ISWC 2026. v2: Added funding acknowledgements and minor layout adjustments; scientific content unchanged

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Privacy Paradox Is a Misnomer: Data Under Structural Uncertainty
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: The infamous privacy paradox refers to the apparent inconsistency between people's stated concern for privacy and their readiness to disclose personal information. This phenomenon has sparked two largely disconnected literatures: one offering experimental evidence of inconsistent behavior, and another providing qualitative accounts and defending the importance of privacy. The Article presents an online field experiment that bridges those literatures and shows that the so-called paradox arises from a mischaracterization of the underlying behavior. The Article finds that it is structural uncertainty about risk that drives seemingly paradoxical privacy decisions. It does so by isolating discounting mechanisms and empirically testing whether observed privacy choices reflect temptation or rational responses to uncertainty. The results suggest that privacy behavior is not paradoxical but, rather, consistent with choices shaped by incomplete information. The Article then discusses the policy implications of this reframing. As privacy decisions stem from structural uncertainty, which operates as a market failure, regulation should aim to reduce that uncertainty. This supports regulation that prioritizes transparency (for people to assess the risks of data collection) and flexibility mechanisms that accommodate evolving contexts. Such reframing provides a new argument for the right to be forgotten, which allows people to revisit prior disclosures as new risks become apparent. By shifting the focus from individual inconsistency to structural uncertainty, the findings call for privacy law to better reflect the reality of people's decision-making environments.

Human-Computer Interaction.title: From Acceptance and Avoidance to Affective Viscosity: Designing Social Agents Intermediating in Human Relationships
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: As social agents become embedded in human relationships, they are expected not only to provide smooth assistance but also to handle rejection, discomfort, jealousy, persistence, and other forms of social tension. This paper connects two research directions: acceptance and avoidance in response to an agent's gaze, approach, and contact, and affective viscosity as a model of how negative affect accumulates, persists, is suppressed, and is expressed over time. We argue that avoidance should not be treated merely as a failure of interaction, but as a relational signal that indicates boundaries between humans and agents. Building on this view, affective viscosity provides a design perspective for agents that maintain, suppress, or express negative states depending on social relationships and interaction histories. We discuss several ongoing design cases, including triadic jealousy, discomfort suppression, patience timing, and spatiotemporal stickiness, and consider how these cases lead to broader questions of blame and accountable intervention. Rather than designing agents as simple scapegoats or artificial villains, we ask how agents can intermediate in problematic social situations while making their intervention traceable, limited, contestable, and repairable.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: The 2nd International Workshop on Trust and Blame in Multi-Person Multi-Agent Societies (TBSA_2nd) in HAI 2026, 5 pages, 2 figures

Human-Computer Interaction.title: Effects of Theory of Mind and Prosocial Beliefs on Steering Human-Aligned Behaviors of LLMs in Ultimatum Games
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in simulating human behaviors and performing theory-of-mind (ToM) reasoning, crucial for complex social interactions. We investigate ToM reasoning's role in aligning agentic behaviors with human norms in negotiation tasks, using the ultimatum game as our referenced task. We initialized LLM agents with different prosocial beliefs (Greedy, Fair, Selfless) and reasoning methods (chain of thought and ToM reasoning of varying levels), examining their decision-making processes and outcomes across multiple LLMs, including reasoning models like o3-mini and DeepSeek-R1 Distilled Qwen 32B. We perform 2,700 simulations to show that ToM reasoning enhances behavioral alignment with human norms, decision-making consistency, and negotiation outcomes. Consistent with prior findings, reasoning LLMs exhibit limited capability compared to ToM-enhanced LLMs, with different game roles benefiting from different ToM orders. Agents almost always chose strategies consistent with their assigned beliefs, and doing so aligned better with human norms in nearly every role, yet Greedy and Selfless agents still fell short of their norms in outcomes. Human verification further revealed that Llama 3.3 70B produces reasoning most consistent with its actions and beliefs. Our findings advance understanding of ToM's role in human-AI interaction and cooperative decision-making. The code used for our experiments can be found at https://github.com/Stealth-py/UltimatumToM.
Human-Computer Interaction.comment: Accepted to AACL-IJCNLP 2026. v2 corrects the RQ4 analysis (Section 5.4, Fig. 4); other results remain unchanged

Human-Computer Interaction.title: The Serendiptionnaire: a Questionnaire for Measuring Experienced Serendipity
Human-Computer Interaction.summary: Serendipity is important to design for, yet it remains difficult to measure and evaluate. No validated questionnaire exists, so studies either borrow ResQue's novelty scale, which does not measure serendipity, or build their own items, which makes findings hard to compare and synthesize. Building on our earlier conceptualization of experienced serendipity as a fortuitous encounter with content that is both refreshing and enriching, we developed the Serendiptionnaire, a questionnaire that operationalizes our framework. We conducted twenty-seven cognitive interviews over three iterations with respondents who varied in age, education level, country of birth, and English proficiency, while they browsed recommendations on platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, and Spotify.
